## Avoid calling CancelScript on Tentacle when StartScript request is still queued

When a script execution is cancelled while the StartScript RPC call is being retried against an offline polling Tentacle, the client currently calls CancelScript on Tentacle even though we can guarantee the script never started there. We need to detect this scenario and cancel the queued request directly, allowing the script execution to stop immediately without attempting to cancel a script that isn't running. This will reduce unnecessary network calls and improve cancellation responsiveness.

13:         /// <summary>
14:         /// Action to Perform before a retry is attempted
15:         /// </summary>
16:         /// <param name="lastException">The last exception that occurred</param>
17:         /// <param name="retrySleepDuration">The duration execution will sleep for before the next retry attempt</param>
18:         /// <param name="retryCount">The current retry count</param>
19:         /// <param name="retryTimeout">The total duration that retries are allowed to take, including the initial execution</param>
20:         /// <param name="elapsedDuration">The duration that has elapsed already including the initial execution and any previous retries</param>
21:         /// <param name="cancellationToken">CancellationToken that will be cancelled when execution is cancelled by the caller</param>
22:         /// <returns></returns>
23:         public delegate Task OnRetryAction(Exception lastException, TimeSpan retrySleepDuration, int retryCount, TimeSpan retryTimeout, TimeSpan elapsedDuration, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
24: 
25:         public delegate Task OnTimeoutAction(TimeSpan retryTimeout, TimeSpan elapsedDuration, int retryCount, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
26: 
27:         public RpcCallRetryHandler(TimeSpan retryTimeout)
28:         {
29:             RetryTimeout = retryTimeout;
30:         }
31: 
32:         public TimeSpan RetryTimeout { get; }
33: 
34:         public TimeSpan RetryIfRemainingDurationAtLeast { get; } = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1);
35: 
36:         public async Task<T> ExecuteWithRetries<T>(
37:             Func<CancellationToken, Task<T>> action,
38:             OnRetryAction? onRetryAction,
39:             OnTimeoutAction? onTimeoutAction,
40:             CancellationToken cancellationToken)
41:         {
42:             Exception? lastException = null;
43:             var started = new Stopwatch();
44:             var nextSleepDuration = TimeSpan.Zero;
45:             var totalRetryCount = 0;
46: 
47:             async Task OnRetryAction(Exception exception, TimeSpan sleepDuration, int retryCount, Context context)
48:             {
49:                 if (lastException == null)
50:                 {
51:                     lastException = exception;
52:                 }
53:                 // Cancellation/Retry Timeout will result in a TransferringRequestCancelledException or ConnectingRequestCancelledException
54:                 // which will hide the original exception. We ignore a cancellation/retry timeout triggered exception so we don't hide the last real exception
55:                 // that occurred during the retry process
56:                 else if(cancellationToken.IsCancellationRequested || !exception.IsConnectingOrTransferringRequestCancelledException())
57:                 {
58:                     lastException = exception;
59:                 }
60:                 
61:                 nextSleepDuration = sleepDuration;
62:                 var elapsedDuration = started.Elapsed;
63:                 var remainingRetryDuration = RetryTimeout - elapsedDuration - sleepDuration;
64: 
65:                 if (ShouldRetryWithRemainingDuration(remainingRetryDuration))
66:                 {
67:                     totalRetryCount = retryCount;
68: 
69:                     if (onRetryAction != null)
70:                     {
71:                         await onRetryAction.Invoke(exception, sleepDuration, retryCount, RetryTimeout, elapsedDuration, cancellationToken).ConfigureAwait(false);
72:                     }
73:                 }
74:             }
75: 
76:             async Task OnTimeoutAction(Context? context, TimeSpan timeout, Task? task, Exception? exception)
77:             {
78:                 var elapsedDuration = started.Elapsed;
79: 
80:                 if (onTimeoutAction != null)
81:                 {
82:                     await onTimeoutAction.Invoke(RetryTimeout, elapsedDuration, totalRetryCount, cancellationToken).ConfigureAwait(false);
83:                 }
84:             }
85: 
86:             var policyBuilder = new RpcCallRetryPolicyBuilder()
87:                 .WithRetryTimeout(RetryTimeout)
88:                 .WithOnRetryAction(OnRetryAction)
89:                 .WithOnTimeoutAction(OnTimeoutAction);
90: 
91:             var retryPolicy = policyBuilder.BuildRetryPolicy();
92:             var isInitialAction = true;
93: 
94:             // This ensures the timeout policy does not apply to the initial request and only applies to retries
95:             async Task<T> ExecuteAction(CancellationToken ct)
96:             {
97:                 if (isInitialAction)
98:                 {
99:                     isInitialAction = false;
100:                     return await action(ct).ConfigureAwait(false);
101:                 }
102: 
103:                 var remainingRetryDuration = RetryTimeout - started.Elapsed - nextSleepDuration;
104: 
105:                 if (!ShouldRetryWithRemainingDuration(remainingRetryDuration))
106:                 {
107:                     // We are short circuiting as the retry duration has elapsed
108:                     await OnTimeoutAction(null, RetryTimeout, null, null).ConfigureAwait(false);
109:                     throw new TimeoutRejectedException("The delegate executed asynchronously through TimeoutPolicy did not complete within the timeout.");
110:                 }
111: 
112:                 var timeoutPolicy = policyBuilder
113:                     // Ensure the remaining retry time excludes the elapsed time
114:                     .WithRetryTimeout(remainingRetryDuration)
115:                     .BuildTimeoutPolicy();
116: 
117:                 return await timeoutPolicy.ExecuteAsync(action, ct).ConfigureAwait(false);
118:             }
119: 
120:             try
121:             {
122:                 started.Start();
123:                 return await retryPolicy.ExecuteAsync(ExecuteAction, cancellationToken);
124:             }
125:             catch (Exception ex) when (ex is TimeoutRejectedException or TaskCanceledException || 
126:                                        ex.IsConnectingOrTransferringRequestCancelledException())

128:                 // If the timeout policy timed out or the cancellation token caused a generic task cancellation 
129:                 // and we have captured an exception from a previous retry, then throw the more meaningful previous exception.
130:                 if (lastException != null)
131:                 {
132:                     throw lastException;
133:                 }
134: 
135:                 throw;
136:             }
137: 
138:             bool ShouldRetryWithRemainingDuration(TimeSpan remainingRetryDuration)
139:             {
140:                 return remainingRetryDuration > RetryIfRemainingDurationAtLeast;
141:             }

Done. Here's what I changed and why.

## Problem

In `ScriptServiceV2Orchestrator.StartScript` and `ScriptServiceV3AlphaOrchestrator.StartScript`, the cancellation-handling was inconsistent about what "the call was still connecting/queued" means:

- `OnErrorAction` (called for each failed retry attempt) already treats **both** `ConnectingRequestCancelledException` **and** `HalibutClientException { ConnectionState: ConnectionState.Connecting }` as "the request never got out" — that's why it decrements `startScriptCallsConnectedCount` for both.
- But the cancellation `catch` only tested `ex is ConnectingRequestCancelledException`.

When StartScript is retried against an offline polling Tentacle, `RpcCallRetryHandler.ExecuteWithRetries` (`Retries/RpcCallRetryHandler.cs:125-136`) rethrows the *earlier* attempt's exception (`lastException`). That rethrown exception is typically a `HalibutClientException` with `ConnectionState.Connecting` (the queued request timed out/cancelled while still in the server's pending-request queue) — not a `ConnectingRequestCancelledException`. So the catch wrongly concluded "not connecting", and ran the full `CancelScript`/`CompleteScript` flow against a Tentacle where the script provably never started.

## Fix

`source/Octopus.Tentacle.Client/Scripts/ScriptServiceV2Orchestrator.cs:110-116` and `.../ScriptServiceV3AlphaOrchestrator.cs:98-104`:

```csharp
var startScriptCallIsConnecting = ex is ConnectingRequestCancelledException ||
    ex is HalibutClientException { ConnectionState: ConnectionState.Connecting };
```

Now both spots agree on the definition of "still queued / never sent". When StartScript was cancelled while still connecting (e.g. queued for an offline polling Tentacle) and no prior attempt actually got out (`startScriptCallsConnectedCount > 1` still safely forces the conservative `CancelScript` path when an earlier attempt may have started the script), the client exits immediately with `OperationCanceledException` — no unnecessary `CancelScript`/`CompleteScript` network calls, and cancellation completes right away. The "cancel the queued request directly" happens inside Halibut via the already-cancelled token that removes the queued request.

## Verification

I could **not** build/run the repo's test suite here: `dotnet restore` fails because the NuGet feeds (feedz.io, nuget.packages.octopushq.com) require proxy auth that isn't available in this environment, and there's no local package cache. What I did verify: the exact edited expression compiles under `LangVersion 9` (the project setting) using the installed Roslyn compiler, and its runtime behavior is correct (matches `ConnectingRequestCancelledException` and Connecting-state `HalibutClientException`, rejects `Transferring`). The `ex is HalibutClientException { ConnectionState: ConnectionState.Connecting }` property pattern was already in use in both files, so no new imports were needed.

Note: the existing `ClientScriptExecutionCanBeCancelledWhenRetriesAreEnabled.DuringStartScript` test's `RetryingCall + Connecting` branch still asserts `CancelScript ≥ 1`, which remains correct — there the retry is forced by killing an *in-flight* response, so the earlier attempt may have started the script and the conservative path stays active. The new (previously buggy) queued-only-retry scenario isn't covered by an existing test; if you can get package restore working I'd recommend adding an integration case where the first StartScript attempt is also cancelled while still queued.

The test project currently only supports generic proxy-based decorators for client services (via `TentacleServiceDecoratorBuilder.RegisterProxyDecorator`). While these work well for applying behavior to all calls (e.g. logging, counting), they are difficult to use when a test needs to customize a single method call — the proxy lacks autocompletion, type safety, and assumes each RPC has exactly one parameter.

    Your task is to add back strongly-typed, per-method decorator builders for the client service interfaces used in integration tests. These builders should allow test writers to easily hook before/after specific methods (e.g. `BeforeCompleteScript`, `DecorateStartScriptWith`) while keeping the existing proxy-based decorators for cross-cutting concerns (like `RecordMethodUsages`).

    The overall design:
    - Create separate builder classes for each client service interface (e.g. `ScriptServiceV2DecoratorBuilder`, `ScriptServiceDecoratorBuilder`, `FileTransferServiceDecoratorBuilder`, `CapabilitiesServiceV2DecoratorBuilder`).
    - Each builder exposes fluent methods like `BeforeXxx(Func<Task>)` or `DecorateXxxWith(delegate)` that wrap the inner service with a strongly-typed decorator.
    - Update `TentacleServiceDecoratorBuilder` to accept these per-method decorators (both as a raw `Decorator<T>` and via an `Action<Builder>` overload) and combine them with the proxy decorators, ensuring the proxy decorators run first (outermost).

We need to enhance the Kubernetes script execution to support running scripts in a user-provided container image, along with the ability to authenticate to private container registries via Kubernetes image pull secrets.

    Currently, `KubernetesJobScriptExecutionContext` is an empty class and the job executor always uses the default container image. The server can now provide execution context with details about a custom container image and optional registry credentials (feed URL, username, password).

    The goals are:

    2. When feed credentials are provided, create a Kubernetes secret in Docker config format (for pulling from private registries) with a deterministic name derived from the feed URL and username.
    3. Attach the secret as an `ImagePullSecrets` entry in the Kubernetes job spec when created.
    4. Use the custom container image (when provided) instead of the default resolved image.

46:                 KubernetesConfig.Namespace,

49:                 watch: true,

51:                 cancellationToken: cancellationToken);
